notes.text: Of Canaan — That is, of the land where most of the Canaanites, strictly so called, now dwelt, which seems to be in the northern part of Canaan. This seems to be of the posterity of that Jabin, whom Joshua slew, Josh. xi, 11, who watched all opportunities to recover his ancient possessions, and to revenge his own and his father's quarrel. In Hazor - In the territory or the kingdom of Hazor, which might now be restored to its former largeness and power. Of the Gentiles - So called, because it was much frequented and inhabited by the Gentiles; either by the Canaanites, who being beaten out of their former possessions, seated themselves in those northern parts; or by other nations coming there for traffick, whence Galilee, where this was, is called Galilee of the Gentiles.
Mightily oppressed — More than former tyrants; from his malice and hatred against the Israelites; and from God's just judgment, the growing punishment being suitable to their aggravated wickedness.

A prophetess — As there were men-prophets, so there were also women-prophetesses, as Miriam, Exod. xv, 20. Huldah, 2 Kings xxii, 14, and divers others; but the word prophets or prophetesses is ambiguous, sometimes being used of persons extraordinarily inspired by God, and endowed with the power of working miracles, and foretelling things to come; and sometimes of persons endowed with special gifts or graces, for the better understanding and discoursing about the word and mind of God. Of this sort were the sons of the prophets, or such as were bred in the schools of the prophets. who are often called prophets, as 1 Sam. x, 5, 10. And because we read nothing of Deborah's miraculous actions, perhaps she was only a woman of eminent holiness, and knowledge of the holy scriptures, by which she was singularly qualified for judging the people according to the laws of God. Judged Israel - That is, determined causes and controversies arising among the Israelites, as is implied, ver. 5. And this Jabin might suffer to be done, especially by a woman. Yet the frequent discharge of this part of the judge's office, whereby she gained great power and authority with the people, did notably (though not observed by the tyrant) prepare the way for her sliding into the other part of her office, which was to defend and rescue the people from their enemies.

And she dwelt — Or, she sat: she had her judgment-seat in the open air, under the shadow of that tree; which was an emblem of the justice she administered there: thriving and growing against opposition, as the palm-tree does under pressures. Came to her - To have their suits and causes determined by her sentence.

Called Barak — By virtue of that power which God had given her, and the people owned in her. Kedesh Naphtali - So called, to distinguish it from other places of that name, one in Judah, and another in Issachar. Hath not the Lord, &c. - That is, assuredly God hath commanded thee; this is not the fancy of a weak woman, which peradventure thou mayst despise; but the command of the great God by my mouth. Mount Tabor - A place most fit for his purpose, as being in the borders of divers tribes, and having a large plain at the top of it, where he might conveniently marshal and discipline his army. Naphtali and Zebulun - These she names because they were nearest and best known to Barak, and therefore soonest brought together, because they were nearest to the enemy, and therefore might speedily be assembled, whilst the other tribes, being at a distance, had better opportunity of gathering forces for their succor; and because these had most smarted under this oppressor, who was in the heart of their country; but these are not named exclusively, as appears by the concurrence of some other tribes.

Draw to Thee — By my secret and powerful providence, ordering and over-ruling his inclinations that way. In fixing the very place, she gave him a sign, which might confirm his faith, when he came to engage.

glossa.text: *And the children of Israel again did evil ((ORIG., hom. 4 in Jud.))* As it were for the sins of the people the good leader died, etc., *as far as* and to Jabin the prince of the Chanaanites.
*Into the hands of Jabin king of Chanaan. ((ADAM., hom. 4 in Jud.))* Jabin the prince of the army, etc., *as far as* either the people of the church be governed, or the sense of each soul.

*Now Debbora was a prophetess. ((ADAM., hom. 5.))* According to the Apostle, etc., *as far as* because it is purity of mind that confers this grace, not diversity of sex.

*Debbora.* A bee, or speech, which signifies a prophet; who composes the sweet honeycombs of heavenly doctrine, and the sweet honey of the divine word. Whence: *How sweet are thy words to my palate, above honey and the honeycomb to my mouth! ((Psal. CXVIII.))* And elsewhere: *The judgments of the Lord,* says the prophet, *are precious above gold and the precious stone exceedingly, and sweeter above honey and the honeycomb. ((Ibid. X.))*

*And she sat under a palm tree,* etc. ((ADAM.)) See in what places prophecy sits, namely, between the high places and the house of God. Nothing lowly, nothing base can be found about the seat of prophecy. As Solomon says: that it stands in the high places, namely in the gates of the cities, or dwells in the ramparts of the walls, or moves freely in high towers. Between the house of God therefore and the high places it is said to dwell. For it does not teach us to seek the things that are upon the earth, but the things that are in heaven, where Christ is, sitting at the right hand of God. Thither it exhorts us to ascend: thither prophecy strives to move her disciples.

notes.text: Look — For supply of their wants, and for help and defense against their oppressors. Until - Until he help and save us. David describes the danger he and his people had been in, ver. 1-5. Blesses God for delivering them, ver. 6-8. A song of degrees of David.

glossa.text: *To thee have I lifted up.* ((ID.)) First the voice of the troubled looking to God, not to other patronages; secondly, he prays for mercy against those who insult him. ((AUG.)) *To thee have I lifted up.* Whither should he lift them, save whither he tended in ascending? this man does not regard himself, as the proud man does who pleases himself: for he who is displeasing to himself, such a one pleases God; and he to whom God is pleasing is himself displeasing to himself. *I have lifted up.* The ascent therefore is in the affection, etc., *as far as* but he who is a pilgrim and desires his country.

*Behold as the eyes,* etc. ((CASS.)) The servant lifts his eyes to the hands of his master, when he is in want or when he is beaten, because both are in the master's power. *As the eyes of the handmaid.* ((AUG.)) *The servant* is the people; *the Lord,* Christ; *the handmaid,* the Church; the mistress, the power of God and the wisdom of God. And though we are now sons and friends by grace, yet we are servants by creation, because every creature serves God. ((CASS.)) He gives a similitude *similttudinem* from the manservant and the handmaid, the master and the mistress, lest the feminine and weaker sex suppose itself excepted.

*Have mercy.* ((ID.)) The second part, where he prays for mercy against those who insult him. The servant who is beaten, having lifted his eyes to God, breaks forth into the needful cry: *Have mercy.*

*We are filled.* As when it is said: What dost thou believe, madman; dost thou see what thou believest? Has anyone returned from the dead, and told thee what is done there? Behold, what I love, I see and enjoy.

notes.text: But of the precise times when this shall be.
For this in general ye do know; and ye can and need know no more.
When they — The men of the world say.
Ye are not in darkness — Sleeping secure in sin.
Awake, and keep awake — Being awakened, let us have all our spiritual senses about us.
They usually sleep and are drunken in the night — These things do not love the light.
God hath not appointed us to wrath — As he hath the obstinately impenitent.
Whether we wake or sleep — Be alive or dead at his coming.

glossa.text: *Of the times.* That is, whether in summer, or in winter, or by day or by night. *And moments.* Namely, at what hour of the day or of the night Christ is to come.

*The day of the Lord.* Here the day is men's, at their own pleasure, but then it will be the day of the Lord. *As a thief.* So unforeseen will he come to the wicked then, which happens also at the death of each one. As a thief, I say not by day but by night, when he comes more secretly, and men sleep, then he steals away all things: so that he who thought himself rich, on waking, may find nothing . So many here well secure will then find that they have nothing of good. For this reason he began concerning the times, that he might warn them to beware for themselves, lest they be so caught.

*For when they shall say.* For, as is found in the words of Daniel: Antichrist and his ministers shall reign three years and a half, and Elias and Enoch shall be slain by him, as is had also in the Apocalypse: And then there shall be such tribulation as was not before, nor shall be after. Afterwards he shall be slain by Michael with the greatest part of his own.

*Sons of light.* Faith is the light which makes the day, that is, the habit of the virtues; on the contrary, darkness is unbelief, night the habit of vices. *We are not of the night nor of darkness,* etc. That is, in things present let us not grow torpid, but let the mind be watchful, considering these fleeting things, and let us use them soberly, not as our own goods but as given for sustenance. Truly we who are not of the night ought not to sleep. For he who sleeps, sleeps because of the night, that is, their vices and their sins have drawn them to this, that, forgetful of eternal life, they rest in these things; and they who are drunken, by using these immoderately; from the night of vices they have this.

*Having put on the breastplate,* etc. As the breastplate guards the vital parts, so faith and charity [guard] us against the appetite of earthly things.

notes.text: Our Lord proceeds by a parable still plainer (if that can be) to declare the final reward of a harmless man. May God give all such in this their day, ears to hear and hearts to understand it! The kingdom of heaven — That is, the King of heaven, Christ. Mark xiii, 34; Luke xix, 12.

To one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one — And who knows whether (all circumstances considered) there be a greater disproportion than this, in the talents of those who have received the most, and those who have received the fewest? According to his own ability - The words may be translated more literally, according to his own mighty power. And immediately took his journey - To heaven.

He that had received one — Made his having fewer talents than others a pretense for not improving any. Went and hid his master's money - Reader, art thou doing the same? Art thou hiding the talent God hath lent thee?

I knew thou art a hard man — No. Thou knowest him not. He never knew God, who thinks him a hard master. Reaping where thou hast not sown - That is, requiring more of us than thou hast given us power to perform. So does every obstinate sinner, in one kind or other, lay the blame of his own sins on God.
And I was afraid — Lest if I had improved my talent, I should have had the more to answer for. So from this fear, one will not learn to read, another will not hear sermons!
Thou knewest — That I require impossibilities! This is not an allowing, but a strong denial of the charge.
Thou oughtest therefore — On that very account, on thy own supposition, to have improved my talent, as far as was possible.
To every one that hath shall be given — So close does God keep to this stated rule, from the beginning to the end of the world. Matt. xiii, 12.

Cast ye the unprofitable servant into the outer darkness — For what? what had he done? It is true he had not done good. But neither is he charged with doing any harm. Why, for this reason, for barely doing no harm, he is consigned to outer darkness. He is pronounced a wicked, because he was a slothful, an unprofitable servant. So mere harmlessness, on which many build their hope of salvation, was the cause of his damnation! There shall be the weeping - Of the careless thoughtless sinner; and the gnashing of teeth - Of the proud and stubborn. The same great truth, that there is no such thing as negative goodness, is in this chapter shown three times:

1. In the parable of the virgins;

2. In the still plainer parable of the servants, who had received the talents; and

3. In a direct unparabolical declaration of the manner wherein our Lord will proceed at the last day. The several parts of each of these exactly answers each other, only each rises above the preceding.

31. When the Son of man shall come in his glory, and all the holy angels with him - With what majesty and grandeur does our Lord here speak of himself Giving us one of the noblest instances of the true sublime. Indeed not many descriptions in the sacred writings themselves seem to equal this. Methinks we can hardly read it without imagining ourselves before the awful tribunal it describes.

glossa.text: *Going into a far country he called his servants,* etc. The place of the flesh is the earth, therefore he led the flesh of Christ, our own, unto foreign parts, when he ascended into heaven.
*And immediately he took his journey.* Not changing place, but allowing them a free power of working.

*He traded with them.* By keeping himself from visible things, by exhorting others as he was able, that they might pass over from visible things to invisible. Or by preaching to both sexes, and by forming them in good morals, he doubled the talents he had received.
*But he reckoned.* He began to examine the deeds of each, their conscience accusing or excusing every one.

*Behold other five.* As many as he converted from error, so many he offered to the Lord, his conscience bearing him witness that by the grace given him he not only profited himself, but also gained those whom he could.

*Over a few things.* The good things of the present life are few, although they seem many, because they are not without an admixture of some trouble. But the eternal good things are many, which are without any trouble of corruption. *Enter into the joy of thy Lord.* Mingled with the choirs of angels: so rejoice within over the gift, that there may now be nothing without over which thou shouldst grieve for corruption.

*He that had received two talents.* This man by his own powers doubled in the Gospel whatever he had learned in the law of God. Or he understood the conscience and the works of the present life as figures of the blessedness to come.
*Thou art a hard man.* Because the way that leads to life is steep, and because the higher the step, the heavier the fall.

*And being afraid I went away,* etc. And fearing to attempt the step of a higher life, lest, seeking another's salvation, I myself should be endangered. *I hid thy talent.* I did not preach what I understood by thy gift.
*Thou knewest that,* etc. Why did that thought not strike fear into thee, so that thou shouldst know that I would seek my own more diligently? What he said by way of excuse is turned into blame.
*To the bankers.* Or to the other teachers, as to the apostles and bishops. Or, to all believers who are able to double the money.

*And give it to him,* etc. We see this for the most part done in the Church, because very many, while they minister well the outward things which they receive, are led on by an added grace to the mystical understanding also.

*For to everyone,* etc. For many, though wise and sharp by nature, if they are slothful, lose the good of nature, and the reward that had been promised them seems to pass over to others, who acquire by industry what they have less of by nature. Or he who has faith and a good will, even if he has less in work, it shall be given to him by the good judge. But he who has it not in faith loses even the virtues which he has naturally, without which [faith] there are no virtues. Or he who has love of the word, to him is given the sense of understanding. But he who has it not, even if he is skilled by natural study, fails. Or he who has not charity loses every good that he has. Note that whatever is given to each in worldly or in spiritual things is reckoned for a talent of which he is to render an account.

places.name: Hazor
places.id: Tell el-Qedah, the largest mound in the southern Levant (c. 200 acres), in the Huleh basin of upper Galilee. The Bronze Age regional capital, named in Egyptian execration texts and the Mari archives; identified by Garstang and excavated by Yadin and Ben-Tor.

places.name: Harosheth of the Gentiles
places.id: Sisera's base, location debated. Tell el-Harbaj at the western end of the Jezreel-Kishon corridor (where the river breaks toward the Bay of Acco) is the traditional candidate; el-Ahwat in the Manasseh hills above the Sharon is a more recent proposal. Either way it commanded the chariot routes from the Sharon to the Jezreel.

places.name: Ramah
places.id: Modern er-Ram on the Jerusalem-Bethel road. Distinct from Ramah of Samuel (Ramathaim-zophim) and from other Ramahs. The fortress mentioned in 1 Kgs 15:17, the place of Jeremiah's lament (Jer 31:15).

places.name: Bethel
places.id: Beitin, a village c. 17 km north of Jerusalem on the central ridge route. Identified by Edward Robinson (1838) and excavated by Albright and Kelso. Earlier called Luz (Joshua 18:13).

places.name: Kedesh
places.id: Tell Qades, in upper Galilee c. 15 km NW of Hazor. Multiple Kedeshes exist; the Joshua 12 listing is identified with Kedesh-Naphtali (cf. Joshua 19:37, 20:7) on the basis of geographic context.

places.name: Mount Tabor
places.id: The conspicuous dome-shaped mountain on the northeast edge of the Jezreel valley. Boundary point between Issachar, Zebulun, and Naphtali; site of Barak's mustering (Judg 4-5). The Hellenistic-Roman fortress on the summit was Itabyrion.

places.name: River Kishon
places.id: The seasonal river draining the Jezreel valley west into the Bay of Acco at the foot of Mount Carmel. The stream-bed is dry most of the year but floods after winter rain; this is the chariot-trap of Judges 4-5.

places.name: Zaanannim
places.id: The 'oak in Zaanannim' is the boundary tree where Heber the Kenite encamped before Sisera was killed (Judg 4:11). Khan et-Tujjar near Mount Tabor has been proposed; the location is uncertain.

echoes.text: Blow the trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm in my holy mountain! Let all the inhabitants of the land tremble, for the day of Yahweh comes, for it is close at hand: A day of darkness and gloominess, a day of clouds and thick darkness. As the dawn spreading on the mountains, a great and strong people; there has never been the like, neither will there be any more after them, even to the years of many generations.
echoes.note: The phrase 'the day of the Lord' (5:2) draws directly on the prophetic Day-of-the-Lord tradition, of which Joel is a primary witness: a day of darkness and gloom announced with alarm. Paul assumes his readers know the concept without explanation, presupposing the prophetic background.

echoes.text: “Woe to you who desire the day of Yahweh! Why do you long for the day of Yahweh? It is darkness, and not light. As if a man fled from a lion, and a bear met him; Or he went into the house and leaned his hand on the wall, and a snake bit him. Won’t the day of Yahweh be darkness, and not light? Even very dark, and no brightness in it?
echoes.note: Amos memorably reframes the day of the Lord as darkness and not light, an inversion that Paul exploits when he contrasts the children of light/day with those overtaken in darkness (5:4-5). The thematic pairing of the Day with darkness and sudden doom is shared.

echoes.text: The great day of Yahweh is near. It is near, and hurries greatly, the voice of the day of Yahweh. The mighty man cries there bitterly. That day is a day of wrath, a day of distress and anguish, a day of trouble and ruin, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness,
echoes.note: Zephaniah describes the day of the Lord as near, hastening, a day of wrath, distress, and ruin coming suddenly. Paul's 'sudden destruction' and the appointment 'not to wrath' (5:3, 9) echo this Day-of-the-Lord wrath vocabulary.

echoes.text: They have healed also the hurt of my people superficially, saying, ‘Peace, peace!’ when there is no peace.
echoes.note: Paul's 'Peace and safety, then sudden destruction' (5:3) inverts the false-prophet slogan 'Peace, peace, when there is no peace.' Jeremiah condemns those who heal the wound lightly by crying peace; Paul makes the same false security the prelude to sudden ruin.

echoes.text: Because, even because they have seduced my people, saying, Peace; and there is no peace; and when one builds up a wall, behold, they plaster it with whitewash:
echoes.note: Ezekiel likewise indicts prophets who say 'Peace' when there is no peace, whitewashing a flimsy wall that will fall. The deceptive cry of peace followed by sudden collapse parallels Paul's 'Peace and safety, then sudden destruction' (5:3).

echoes.text: They will be dismayed. Pangs and sorrows will seize them. They will be in pain like a woman in labor. They will look in amazement one at another. Their faces will be faces of flame.
echoes.note: Paul compares the sudden destruction to 'birth pains on a pregnant woman' (5:3). Isaiah's oracle on the day of the Lord against Babylon uses the same labor-pang simile for inescapable terror, tying the metaphor directly to a Day-of-the-Lord context.

echoes.text: He put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head; and he put on garments of vengeance for clothing, and was clad with zeal as a mantle.
echoes.note: The armor metaphor 'breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation' (5:8) reworks Isaiah's portrait of the Divine Warrior who 'put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head.' Paul transfers God's own armor to the believer and recasts the virtues.

echoes.text: “For, behold, the day comes, it burns as a furnace; and all the proud, and all who work wickedness, will be stubble; and the day that comes will burn them up,” says Yahweh of Armies, “that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.
echoes.note: Malachi's coming day burning like an oven that overtakes the wicked contributes to the burning, inescapable judgment color of Paul's Day-of-the-Lord imagery (5:2-3). Faint and one of several Day texts standing behind the motif.

echoes.text: They have healed the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace.
echoes.note: A near-doublet of Jer 6:14, again denouncing 'Peace, peace, when there is no peace.' It reinforces the false-peace background of the 'Peace and safety' slogan in 5:3.

echoes.text: Like as a woman with child, who draws near the time of her delivery, is in pain and cries out in her pangs; so we have been before you, Yahweh.
echoes.note: Isaiah pictures a pregnant woman writhing and crying out in her labor pains as an image of distress, a standard prophetic figure that informs Paul's labor-pain simile for sudden destruction (5:3).

echoes.text: We have heard its report; our hands become feeble: anguish has taken hold of us, and pains as of a woman in labor.
echoes.note: Jeremiah describes anguish and pain 'like a woman in labor' on hearing of coming disaster, in the same context as the false-peace slogan of 6:14. The shared labor-pang imagery for sudden, inescapable calamity stands behind 5:3.

echoes.text: He will put on righteousness as a breastplate, And will array himself with judgement unfeigned as with a helmet;
echoes.note: Wisdom, itself dependent on Isa 59:17, depicts the Lord taking 'holiness as an invincible shield' and putting on righteousness as a breastplate, arming creation against enemies. It is a likely mediating deuterocanonical witness for Paul's armor imagery in 5:8.

echoes.text: House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of Yahweh.
echoes.note: Isaiah's call to 'walk in the light of the LORD' offers a faint background for Paul's 'children of light... children of the day' (5:5) language of belonging to the light rather than darkness. Contested and one of several light/darkness texts.

echoes.text: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and Yahweh’s glory is risen on you. For, behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the peoples; but Yahweh will arise on you, and his glory shall be seen on you. Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising.
echoes.note: Isaiah's eschatological light shining on God's people while darkness covers the nations supplies a faint backdrop to the light/day versus night/darkness antithesis of 5:4-5. Faint and figural rather than verbal.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Joseph found favor in his sight. He ministered to him, and he made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand. From the time that he made him overseer in his house, and over all that he had, Yahweh blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake. Yahweh’s blessing was on all that he had, in the house and in the field. He left all that he had in Joseph’s hand. He didn’t concern himself with anything, except for the food which he […]
echoes.note: Joseph entrusted with all his master's goods and proving faithful as a steward supplies a narrative type of the trusted servant set over his lord's property, rewarded with greater authority.

echoes.text: Go to the ant, you sluggard. Consider her ways, and be wise; which having no chief, overseer, or ruler, provides her bread in the summer, and gathers her food in the harvest. How long will you sleep, sluggard? When will you arise out of your sleep? A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: so your poverty will come as a robber, and your scarcity as an armed man.
echoes.note: The condemnation of the 'slothful' servant (v.26) and the praise of diligent gain echoes wisdom's contrast between the industrious and the sluggard whose laziness brings ruin.

echoes.text: He becomes poor who works with a lazy hand, but the hand of the diligent brings wealth. He who gathers in summer is a wise son, but he who sleeps during the harvest is a son who causes shame.
echoes.note: 'A slack hand causes poverty, but the hand of the diligent makes rich; he who gathers in summer is a prudent son' undergirds the parable's reward of the productive servants and reproach of the one who buried his trust.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt. Those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the expanse; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever.
echoes.note: The judgment-language of the parable's frame (joy of the lord vs. outer darkness) participates in the apocalyptic two-fold destiny of the wise who shine and others who go to shame, the eschatological backdrop Matthew assumes.

echoes.text: Behold, all you who kindle a fire, who adorn yourselves with torches around yourselves; walk in the flame of your fire, and among the brands that you have kindled. You shall have this of my hand; you shall lie down in sorrow.
echoes.note: The motif of being cast into darkness as judgment ('you shall lie down in torment') faintly underlies the 'outer darkness, weeping and gnashing of teeth' fate of the unprofitable servant.

notes.text: Hold thy peace — Thou that murmurest against God, stand in awe. The day - A day of vengeance from the Lord. A sacrifice - The wicked Jews, whom he will sacrifice by the sword. His guests - summoned the beasts of the field, and the fowls of the air, to eat the flesh, and drink the blood.

Dwelling place — Although we and our fathers, for some generations, have had no fixed habitation, yet thou hast been instead of a dwelling-place to us, by thy watchful and gracious providence. And this intimates that all the following miseries were not to be imputed to God but themselves.
Thou — Thou hadst thy power, and all thy perfections, from all eternity.

Turnedst — But as for man, his case is far otherwise, though he was made by thee happy. and immortal, yet for his sin thou didst make him mortal and miserable. Saidst - Didst pronounce that sad sentence, return, O men, to the dust out of which ye were taken, Gen. iii, 19.
Past — Indeed time seems long when it is to come, but when it is past, very short and contemptible. A watch - Which lasted but three or four hours.
Them — Mankind. Away - Universally, without exception or distinction. A sleep - Short and vain, as sleep is, and not minded 'till it be past.
Are consumed — Thou dost not suffer us to live so long as we might by the course of nature.
Hast set — Thou dost observe them, as a righteous judge, and art calling us to an account for them. Secret sins - Which though hid from the eyes of men, thou hast brought to light by thy judgments.

glossa.text:
*A prayer of Moses.* ((AUG.)) When the old life and the new, etc., *as far as* and he sees wonders out of the law of God.

((CASS., REM.)) This psalm treats of the failing of the human race, which shall be taken away through Christ.

*O Lord, a refuge.* ((CASS.)) First, he sets forth an eternal refuge for man in time.

*Before the mountains.* But lest he should seem not to have been, before he was a refuge to us, he adds *before. The mountains, the earth.* ((AUG.)) Behold, every rational creature is distinguished *Elcce* by this difference, that by the name *of mountains* is meant the loftiness of the angels; and by the name *of the earth* the lowliness of men: and therefore not unfittingly did he so distinguish the words, that he should say that *the mountains,* that is, the angels, *were made,* and that *the earth,* that is, men, *was formed. They should be made, or it should be formed.* To be formed, or fashioned, is wont to be said of bodies: to be made, out of nothing. *From the world.* He would more fitly say, etc., *as far as* but here *the world* is put for the eternal. *From the world.* Behold what eternity is a refuge to us, etc., *as far as: Turn not away, for a thousand years. Thou art.* Excellently does he say it, because he is unchangeable. He does not say thou shalt be, or thou wast, since the unchangeable essence of God has not known the past, or the future; whence it is said: *I am who am.* And, *He who is hath sent me to you?* And: *But thou art the selfsame, and thy years shall not fail.* *aani*

*Turn not away.* ((CASS.)) Secondly, he sets out the infirmity of man, for which he asks that help be brought. *Unto lowliness.* That is, earthly concupiscence, etc., *as far as* who taught us to seek the things of heaven.
*Yesterday's day.* ((AUG.)) He does not say, at least as tomorrow's, etc., *as far as* in anxiety, and trembling, as nothing *qnasi*.

*In the morning as grass.* ((AUG., CASS.)) Let it be changed from the quality of the night.

*In the evening let it fall.* Cut down, or broken, at the last. ((CASS.)) *In the morning as grass.* I have said that the years are held, etc., *as far as* the youth which flowers and passes away.

 *In the evening.* Old age, when the vigour of a man grows cold. *Or, in the morning as grass.* A fitting comparison, as if to say, as grass is changed from the quality which it has in the night, to a worse one in the morning when the sun is risen: so is a man changed for the worse.

*We have failed in thy wrath, and in thy fury we have been troubled.* ((AUG.)) Made mortal and liable to suffering, which nevertheless we fear to end by death, whence follows: *And in thy fury we have been troubled. The world.* Our depraved life. Or *the world,* those who come after. *In the enlightening of the countenance.* ((CASS.)) Those things are covered which have pardon: those are *enlightened* which are punished.

notes.text: But of the precise times when this shall be.
For this in general ye do know; and ye can and need know no more.
When they — The men of the world say.
Ye are not in darkness — Sleeping secure in sin.
Awake, and keep awake — Being awakened, let us have all our spiritual senses about us.
They usually sleep and are drunken in the night — These things do not love the light.
God hath not appointed us to wrath — As he hath the obstinately impenitent.
Whether we wake or sleep — Be alive or dead at his coming.

glossa.text: *Of the times.* That is, whether in summer, or in winter, or by day or by night. *And moments.* Namely, at what hour of the day or of the night Christ is to come.

*The day of the Lord.* Here the day is men's, at their own pleasure, but then it will be the day of the Lord. *As a thief.* So unforeseen will he come to the wicked then, which happens also at the death of each one. As a thief, I say not by day but by night, when he comes more secretly, and men sleep, then he steals away all things: so that he who thought himself rich, on waking, may find nothing . So many here well secure will then find that they have nothing of good. For this reason he began concerning the times, that he might warn them to beware for themselves, lest they be so caught.

*For when they shall say.* For, as is found in the words of Daniel: Antichrist and his ministers shall reign three years and a half, and Elias and Enoch shall be slain by him, as is had also in the Apocalypse: And then there shall be such tribulation as was not before, nor shall be after. Afterwards he shall be slain by Michael with the greatest part of his own.

*Sons of light.* Faith is the light which makes the day, that is, the habit of the virtues; on the contrary, darkness is unbelief, night the habit of vices. *We are not of the night nor of darkness,* etc. That is, in things present let us not grow torpid, but let the mind be watchful, considering these fleeting things, and let us use them soberly, not as our own goods but as given for sustenance. Truly we who are not of the night ought not to sleep. For he who sleeps, sleeps because of the night, that is, their vices and their sins have drawn them to this, that, forgetful of eternal life, they rest in these things; and they who are drunken, by using these immoderately; from the night of vices they have this.

*Having put on the breastplate,* etc. As the breastplate guards the vital parts, so faith and charity [guard] us against the appetite of earthly things.

notes.text: Our Lord proceeds by a parable still plainer (if that can be) to declare the final reward of a harmless man. May God give all such in this their day, ears to hear and hearts to understand it! The kingdom of heaven — That is, the King of heaven, Christ. Mark xiii, 34; Luke xix, 12.

To one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one — And who knows whether (all circumstances considered) there be a greater disproportion than this, in the talents of those who have received the most, and those who have received the fewest? According to his own ability - The words may be translated more literally, according to his own mighty power. And immediately took his journey - To heaven.

He that had received one — Made his having fewer talents than others a pretense for not improving any. Went and hid his master's money - Reader, art thou doing the same? Art thou hiding the talent God hath lent thee?

I knew thou art a hard man — No. Thou knowest him not. He never knew God, who thinks him a hard master. Reaping where thou hast not sown - That is, requiring more of us than thou hast given us power to perform. So does every obstinate sinner, in one kind or other, lay the blame of his own sins on God.
And I was afraid — Lest if I had improved my talent, I should have had the more to answer for. So from this fear, one will not learn to read, another will not hear sermons!
Thou knewest — That I require impossibilities! This is not an allowing, but a strong denial of the charge.
Thou oughtest therefore — On that very account, on thy own supposition, to have improved my talent, as far as was possible.
To every one that hath shall be given — So close does God keep to this stated rule, from the beginning to the end of the world. Matt. xiii, 12.

Cast ye the unprofitable servant into the outer darkness — For what? what had he done? It is true he had not done good. But neither is he charged with doing any harm. Why, for this reason, for barely doing no harm, he is consigned to outer darkness. He is pronounced a wicked, because he was a slothful, an unprofitable servant. So mere harmlessness, on which many build their hope of salvation, was the cause of his damnation! There shall be the weeping - Of the careless thoughtless sinner; and the gnashing of teeth - Of the proud and stubborn. The same great truth, that there is no such thing as negative goodness, is in this chapter shown three times:

1. In the parable of the virgins;

2. In the still plainer parable of the servants, who had received the talents; and

3. In a direct unparabolical declaration of the manner wherein our Lord will proceed at the last day. The several parts of each of these exactly answers each other, only each rises above the preceding.

31. When the Son of man shall come in his glory, and all the holy angels with him - With what majesty and grandeur does our Lord here speak of himself Giving us one of the noblest instances of the true sublime. Indeed not many descriptions in the sacred writings themselves seem to equal this. Methinks we can hardly read it without imagining ourselves before the awful tribunal it describes.

glossa.text: *Going into a far country he called his servants,* etc. The place of the flesh is the earth, therefore he led the flesh of Christ, our own, unto foreign parts, when he ascended into heaven.
*And immediately he took his journey.* Not changing place, but allowing them a free power of working.

*He traded with them.* By keeping himself from visible things, by exhorting others as he was able, that they might pass over from visible things to invisible. Or by preaching to both sexes, and by forming them in good morals, he doubled the talents he had received.
*But he reckoned.* He began to examine the deeds of each, their conscience accusing or excusing every one.

*Behold other five.* As many as he converted from error, so many he offered to the Lord, his conscience bearing him witness that by the grace given him he not only profited himself, but also gained those whom he could.

*Over a few things.* The good things of the present life are few, although they seem many, because they are not without an admixture of some trouble. But the eternal good things are many, which are without any trouble of corruption. *Enter into the joy of thy Lord.* Mingled with the choirs of angels: so rejoice within over the gift, that there may now be nothing without over which thou shouldst grieve for corruption.

*He that had received two talents.* This man by his own powers doubled in the Gospel whatever he had learned in the law of God. Or he understood the conscience and the works of the present life as figures of the blessedness to come.
*Thou art a hard man.* Because the way that leads to life is steep, and because the higher the step, the heavier the fall.

*And being afraid I went away,* etc. And fearing to attempt the step of a higher life, lest, seeking another's salvation, I myself should be endangered. *I hid thy talent.* I did not preach what I understood by thy gift.
*Thou knewest that,* etc. Why did that thought not strike fear into thee, so that thou shouldst know that I would seek my own more diligently? What he said by way of excuse is turned into blame.
*To the bankers.* Or to the other teachers, as to the apostles and bishops. Or, to all believers who are able to double the money.

*And give it to him,* etc. We see this for the most part done in the Church, because very many, while they minister well the outward things which they receive, are led on by an added grace to the mystical understanding also.

*For to everyone,* etc. For many, though wise and sharp by nature, if they are slothful, lose the good of nature, and the reward that had been promised them seems to pass over to others, who acquire by industry what they have less of by nature. Or he who has faith and a good will, even if he has less in work, it shall be given to him by the good judge. But he who has it not in faith loses even the virtues which he has naturally, without which [faith] there are no virtues. Or he who has love of the word, to him is given the sense of understanding. But he who has it not, even if he is skilled by natural study, fails. Or he who has not charity loses every good that he has. Note that whatever is given to each in worldly or in spiritual things is reckoned for a talent of which he is to render an account.

hymns.title: Christ, mighty Savior, Light of all creation
Day is dying in the west
Fix me for my long white robe
O God, our help in ages past
God, that madest earth and heaven

echoes.text: Blow the trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm in my holy mountain! Let all the inhabitants of the land tremble, for the day of Yahweh comes, for it is close at hand: A day of darkness and gloominess, a day of clouds and thick darkness. As the dawn spreading on the mountains, a great and strong people; there has never been the like, neither will there be any more after them, even to the years of many generations.
echoes.note: The phrase 'the day of the Lord' (5:2) draws directly on the prophetic Day-of-the-Lord tradition, of which Joel is a primary witness: a day of darkness and gloom announced with alarm. Paul assumes his readers know the concept without explanation, presupposing the prophetic background.

echoes.text: “Woe to you who desire the day of Yahweh! Why do you long for the day of Yahweh? It is darkness, and not light. As if a man fled from a lion, and a bear met him; Or he went into the house and leaned his hand on the wall, and a snake bit him. Won’t the day of Yahweh be darkness, and not light? Even very dark, and no brightness in it?
echoes.note: Amos memorably reframes the day of the Lord as darkness and not light, an inversion that Paul exploits when he contrasts the children of light/day with those overtaken in darkness (5:4-5). The thematic pairing of the Day with darkness and sudden doom is shared.

echoes.text: The great day of Yahweh is near. It is near, and hurries greatly, the voice of the day of Yahweh. The mighty man cries there bitterly. That day is a day of wrath, a day of distress and anguish, a day of trouble and ruin, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness,
echoes.note: Zephaniah describes the day of the Lord as near, hastening, a day of wrath, distress, and ruin coming suddenly. Paul's 'sudden destruction' and the appointment 'not to wrath' (5:3, 9) echo this Day-of-the-Lord wrath vocabulary.

echoes.text: They have healed also the hurt of my people superficially, saying, ‘Peace, peace!’ when there is no peace.
echoes.note: Paul's 'Peace and safety, then sudden destruction' (5:3) inverts the false-prophet slogan 'Peace, peace, when there is no peace.' Jeremiah condemns those who heal the wound lightly by crying peace; Paul makes the same false security the prelude to sudden ruin.

echoes.text: Because, even because they have seduced my people, saying, Peace; and there is no peace; and when one builds up a wall, behold, they plaster it with whitewash:
echoes.note: Ezekiel likewise indicts prophets who say 'Peace' when there is no peace, whitewashing a flimsy wall that will fall. The deceptive cry of peace followed by sudden collapse parallels Paul's 'Peace and safety, then sudden destruction' (5:3).

echoes.text: They will be dismayed. Pangs and sorrows will seize them. They will be in pain like a woman in labor. They will look in amazement one at another. Their faces will be faces of flame.
echoes.note: Paul compares the sudden destruction to 'birth pains on a pregnant woman' (5:3). Isaiah's oracle on the day of the Lord against Babylon uses the same labor-pang simile for inescapable terror, tying the metaphor directly to a Day-of-the-Lord context.

echoes.text: He put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head; and he put on garments of vengeance for clothing, and was clad with zeal as a mantle.
echoes.note: The armor metaphor 'breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation' (5:8) reworks Isaiah's portrait of the Divine Warrior who 'put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head.' Paul transfers God's own armor to the believer and recasts the virtues.

echoes.text: “For, behold, the day comes, it burns as a furnace; and all the proud, and all who work wickedness, will be stubble; and the day that comes will burn them up,” says Yahweh of Armies, “that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.
echoes.note: Malachi's coming day burning like an oven that overtakes the wicked contributes to the burning, inescapable judgment color of Paul's Day-of-the-Lord imagery (5:2-3). Faint and one of several Day texts standing behind the motif.

echoes.text: They have healed the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace.
echoes.note: A near-doublet of Jer 6:14, again denouncing 'Peace, peace, when there is no peace.' It reinforces the false-peace background of the 'Peace and safety' slogan in 5:3.

echoes.text: Like as a woman with child, who draws near the time of her delivery, is in pain and cries out in her pangs; so we have been before you, Yahweh.
echoes.note: Isaiah pictures a pregnant woman writhing and crying out in her labor pains as an image of distress, a standard prophetic figure that informs Paul's labor-pain simile for sudden destruction (5:3).

echoes.text: We have heard its report; our hands become feeble: anguish has taken hold of us, and pains as of a woman in labor.
echoes.note: Jeremiah describes anguish and pain 'like a woman in labor' on hearing of coming disaster, in the same context as the false-peace slogan of 6:14. The shared labor-pang imagery for sudden, inescapable calamity stands behind 5:3.

echoes.text: He will put on righteousness as a breastplate, And will array himself with judgement unfeigned as with a helmet;
echoes.note: Wisdom, itself dependent on Isa 59:17, depicts the Lord taking 'holiness as an invincible shield' and putting on righteousness as a breastplate, arming creation against enemies. It is a likely mediating deuterocanonical witness for Paul's armor imagery in 5:8.

echoes.text: House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of Yahweh.
echoes.note: Isaiah's call to 'walk in the light of the LORD' offers a faint background for Paul's 'children of light... children of the day' (5:5) language of belonging to the light rather than darkness. Contested and one of several light/darkness texts.

echoes.text: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and Yahweh’s glory is risen on you. For, behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the peoples; but Yahweh will arise on you, and his glory shall be seen on you. Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising.
echoes.note: Isaiah's eschatological light shining on God's people while darkness covers the nations supplies a faint backdrop to the light/day versus night/darkness antithesis of 5:4-5. Faint and figural rather than verbal.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Joseph found favor in his sight. He ministered to him, and he made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand. From the time that he made him overseer in his house, and over all that he had, Yahweh blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake. Yahweh’s blessing was on all that he had, in the house and in the field. He left all that he had in Joseph’s hand. He didn’t concern himself with anything, except for the food which he […]
echoes.note: Joseph entrusted with all his master's goods and proving faithful as a steward supplies a narrative type of the trusted servant set over his lord's property, rewarded with greater authority.

echoes.text: Go to the ant, you sluggard. Consider her ways, and be wise; which having no chief, overseer, or ruler, provides her bread in the summer, and gathers her food in the harvest. How long will you sleep, sluggard? When will you arise out of your sleep? A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: so your poverty will come as a robber, and your scarcity as an armed man.
echoes.note: The condemnation of the 'slothful' servant (v.26) and the praise of diligent gain echoes wisdom's contrast between the industrious and the sluggard whose laziness brings ruin.

echoes.text: He becomes poor who works with a lazy hand, but the hand of the diligent brings wealth. He who gathers in summer is a wise son, but he who sleeps during the harvest is a son who causes shame.
echoes.note: 'A slack hand causes poverty, but the hand of the diligent makes rich; he who gathers in summer is a prudent son' undergirds the parable's reward of the productive servants and reproach of the one who buried his trust.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt. Those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the expanse; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever.
echoes.note: The judgment-language of the parable's frame (joy of the lord vs. outer darkness) participates in the apocalyptic two-fold destiny of the wise who shine and others who go to shame, the eschatological backdrop Matthew assumes.

echoes.text: Behold, all you who kindle a fire, who adorn yourselves with torches around yourselves; walk in the flame of your fire, and among the brands that you have kindled. You shall have this of my hand; you shall lie down in sorrow.
echoes.note: The motif of being cast into darkness as judgment ('you shall lie down in torment') faintly underlies the 'outer darkness, weeping and gnashing of teeth' fate of the unprofitable servant.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Lord, you have been our dwelling place in all generations.
Teach us to number our days, that we may gain wise hearts.
To one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one.
Well done, good and faithful servant.
The day of the Lord is near; do not bury what God has given.
We will trade in love while there is light.
Come, let us worship the God of all our days.
We come to spend our lives well. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Our years pass like grass that springs up in the morning and fades by night; before the mountains were born, you are God.
Teach us to number our days, O God.
Into our hands you have placed a treasure — a life, a gift, a measure of grace — not to be buried in the ground but put to work.
Teach us to number our days, O God.
The day draws near; do not hide your light, do not bury your gift in fear.
Teach us to number our days, O God.
Spend what you have been given, and hear the welcome: well done, good and faithful servant; enter the joy of your master.
Teach us to number our days, O God.
So come, children of the light, and worship while it is day.
Teach us to number our days, O God. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: You have been our dwelling place in every generation.
Teach us to number our days.
To each was given a treasure to put to work.
Teach us to number our days.
Do not bury the gift; the day is near.
Teach us to number our days.
Come, let us spend our lives in worship.
We come to live them well. Amen.
